elements.quote: This meta-­ analysis aimed to evaluate the association between adherence to a Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome among children and adolescents.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly describes the work as a meta-analysis.

elements.quote: This meta-­ analysis aimed to evaluate the association between adherence to a Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome among children and adolescents.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an explicit stated objective (evaluate the association).

elements.quote: Studies were included if they evaluated the association between adherence to a Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome among children and adolescents.
elements.reason: The abstract states an inclusion criterion, but does not specify inclusion/exclusion criteria comprehensively (e.g., no explicit exclusion criteria).
The abstract does not identify information sources used to identify studies nor when each source was last searched.
The abstract does not describe methods used to assess risk of bias.

elements.quote: A random-­ effects model was used to estimate the summary effect size.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the method used to synthesize/present results (random-effects meta-analytic model).

elements.quote: A total of eight studies involving children and adolescents aged 6 to 19 years were included in the meta-­ analysis (n=6562, 50% girls).
elements.reason: The abstract reports total included studies and participants and gives relevant participant characteristics (age range and sex proportion).

elements.quote: Low adherence to the Mediterranean diet was associated with greater odds of metabolic syndrome than was medium/high adherence (odds ratio [OR] = 2.18, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.45 to 3.28; p < 0.001; inconsistency index [ I 2 ] = 64.15%).
elements.reason: The abstract provides results for the main outcome including an effect estimate (OR with 95% CI) and related statistics.

elements.quote: Low adherence to the Mediterranean diet was associated with greater odds of metabolic syndrome than was medium/high adherence (odds ratio [OR] = 2.18, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.45 to 3.28; p < 0.001; inconsistency index [ I 2 ] = 64.15%).
elements.reason: Because a meta-analysis was conducted, the abstract reports the summary estimate (OR) and its confidence interval.

elements.quote: Low adherence to the Mediterranean diet was associated with greater odds of metabolic syndrome than was medium/high adherence
elements.reason: The abstract indicates the direction of effect (low adherence has greater odds of MetS than medium/high adherence), implying medium/high adherence is favored.
The abstract does not briefly summarize important limitations of the included evidence (e.g., risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision) as part of the abstract content provided.

elements.quote: This meta-­ analysis suggested that increased adherence to a Mediterranean diet is associated with lower probabilities of having cardiometabolic risk among children and adolescents.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results.
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding for the review.
Although protocol registration information appears in retrieved Methods text, it is not reported within the provided abstract text evidence.

elements.quote: Background The Mediterranean diet has been associated with improved metabolic health among adults.
elements.reason: Provides some context on existing knowledge (associations in adults), but does not describe important uncertainties or gaps in knowledge for children/adolescents.

elements.quote: This meta-­ analysis aimed to evaluate the association between adherence to a Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome among children and adolescents.
elements.reason: Explains the objective of the review, indicating a need to evaluate the association in children/adolescents, but does not explicitly state the importance/need for conducting the review in the context of unanswered questions or limitations of existing evidence.
No evidence was retrieved describing similar systematic reviews or explaining how this review differs (e.g., updates/replications with citations).
The retrieved evidence does not describe a proposed mechanism of action of an intervention, which is required only for intervention-effect reviews.
No logic model or hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes were retrieved.

The retrieved evidence does not include an explicit statement of the review objective(s) or question(s) using a relevant question-formulation framework; it only describes methods, eligibility criteria, and effect measures.

elements.quote: All studies were included in the meta-­ analysis to assess the association between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS among children and adolescents.
elements.reason: The review appears to assess an association (using odds ratios) rather than planned intervention effects; therefore PICO-style planned comparisons for intervention effects are not applicable based on the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: To be eligible for inclusion in the present review, studies needed to meet the following criteria: (i) were children or adolescents aged 5-19 years, all countries and ethnic backgrounds; (ii) had a MetS outcome; (iii) had an adherence to the MedDiet assessed by a validated questionnaire; and (iv) had a longitudinal and cross-­ sectional study design.
elements.reason: Eligibility specifies key study characteristics (population age 5–19, outcome MetS, exposure assessed with a validated questionnaire, and eligible study designs including longitudinal and cross-sectional). However, follow-up requirements are not specified.

elements.quote: Furthermore, the need to convert data for the purpose of quantitative analysis presents an additional limitation to our study; additionally, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English.
elements.reason: The review specifies a language restriction (published in English), but dissemination year and publication/report status are not reported in the retrieved evidence.
The retrieved evidence does not distinguish exclusions based on (a) outcomes not measured versus (b) outcome results not reported.
The retrieved evidence does not specify the groups used in each synthesis and how they were linked to the comparisons in the review objectives.

elements.quote: However, to narrow the scope of the meta-­ analysis, only studies that associated the MedDiet with the outcome of MetS were included.
elements.reason: A rationale is provided for a notable eligibility restriction (including only studies that associated MedDiet with MetS to narrow the scope). No further rationale for other restrictions is provided in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: The searches included studies published from database inception to 22 April 2024.
elements.reason: The end date for the database searches (22 April 2024) is reported.

elements.quote: Two authors independently conducted systematic searches in the following databases: Excerpta Medica Database (Embase, via OvidSP), Scopus, Web of Science and PubMed. The searches included studies published from database inception to 22 April 2024.

No study registers/regulatory databases/online repositories searched are reported in the provided evidence.
No websites/search engines/other online sources searched are reported in the provided evidence.

When two studies used duplicate data from the same source and year, the study with the larger sample size was selected.

elements.quote: A sensitivity analysis was conducted by sequentially omitting one study at a time to assess the robustness of the overall effect estimate. These findings indicate that no single study unduly influenced the overall results, supporting the robustness of the association between low adherence to the MedDiet and higher odds of MetS in children and adolescents (figure 4).

elements.quote: We identified 3775 articles by searching the databases MEDLINE (via PubMed), Embase (Ovid) and Web of Science. A total of 1456 studies were excluded because of duplication, while 1565 were classified as ineligible by automation tools. Another 546 studies were removed for additional reasons. We examined the titles and abstracts of 208 studies and excluded 157 on the basis of our findings. We screened 51 articles for eligibility. Eight studies were included in the meta-­ analysis.

elements.quote: These findings are consistent with previous research in adults, suggesting that adherence to the MedDiet may have favourable effects on MetS outcomes. 17 However, unlike the study performed by Bakaloudi et al , 17 our study focused only on children and adolescents, presenting a well-­ designed systematic review and meta-­ analysis of paediatric populations.

elements.quote: Limitations of the present systematic review include the fact that the degree of adherence to the MedDiet could be subject to regional variations, potentially introducing further biases. For example, individuals with high adherence to the MedDiet living in Mediterranean areas may consume certain foods more frequently than may those residing in non-­ Mediterranean regions. Furthermore, the need to convert data for the purpose of quantitative analysis presents an additional limitation to our study; additionally, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English. In addition, most of the included studies were cross-­ sectional, which limits the ability to establish causality or determine the temporal relationship between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS outcomes. However, further well-­ designed prospective cohort studies and randomised controlled trials are needed to confirm the findings of our meta-­ analysis and elucidate the underlying mechanisms involved. All the studies used a cross-­ sectional design, so the observed results should be interpreted with caution. Another significant limitation is that studies use different questionnaires to determine adherence to the MedDiet, as well as different points for comparisons between categories. Additionally, there is no single criterion for defining MetS in the paediatric population, so the observed inconsistency could be due to these limitations. Finally, a formal assessment of the certainty of evidence (eg, using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach) was not performed, as this was beyond the scope of the present review.
elements.reason: The Discussion explicitly describes multiple limitations of the included evidence (e.g., cross-sectional design limiting causality, regional variation, conversion of data, language restriction, different adherence questionnaires and MetS definitions, and lack of certainty-of-evidence assessment).
